summary: This standards-track RFC defines HTTP status code 451, which a server can use to say that access to a resource is denied because of a legal demand, such as a court order or government request. It lets clients and users tell legal blocking apart from ordinary errors like 403 Forbidden.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP status 451 tells a client that access was denied because of a legal demand. The response should explain the demand and can identify the entity that is blocking access.

questions: http status code for legal blocking
what does 451 unavailable for legal reasons mean
what is the blocked-by link relation
subtitle: HTTP status 451 identifies access denied because of a legal demand.

tldr.problem: A user may not be able to tell when a server denies access because of a legal demand.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP status 451 reports a legal denial, and a blocked-by Link relation can identify the entity implementing the block.
tldr.outcome: The code can make legal restrictions visible, but clients cannot rely on servers using it.

today: RFC 7725 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Making Legal Restrictions Visible
sections.content: RFC 7725 defines an HTTP status code for cases where a server operator has received a legal demand to deny access to a resource. The code can make legal or public-policy restrictions on server operations more transparent to operators and users.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can use a specific status code when a legal demand causes it to deny access. This helps distinguish that reason from other reasons for a failed request.

sections.title: 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons
sections.content:
Status 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons means that access is denied because of a legal demand. The responding server may be an ISP or search engine rather than the origin server. Responses SHOULD explain the demand in the body, including who made it, the relevant law or regulation, and the people and resources it covers.

A 451 response does not say whether the requested resource exists. It is cacheable by default unless the method definition or explicit cache controls say otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: A 451 response says that a legal demand caused the denial, but it does not confirm whether the resource exists. The response should explain who made the demand and what it covers.

sections.title: Identifying the Blocking Entity
sections.content:
The entity that blocks access may be an ISP, cache provider or DNS server, and may not be the origin server. When a blocking entity returns 451, it SHOULD include a Link header with a URI reference identifying itself. The header MUST use the relation value blocked-by.

The link identifies the entity implementing the block, not another entity that demanded it. The response body is the place to discuss administrative and policy details.
sections.plainLanguage: The Link header can name the organization or system that actually blocks the request. The response body can explain the legal or policy details.

sections.title: Limits and Registrations
sections.content: Clients cannot rely on receiving status 451 because legal authorities may demand both restricted access and secrecy about that demand. IANA registered status code 451 and the blocked-by Link relation.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may not disclose that a legal demand caused a block, so a client cannot rely on seeing 451. IANA registered the status code and link relation.
